Summary: The paper builds a controlled comparison of generation strategies for writing OMIM phenotype entries from exactly the papers the curators cited (100 entries with 2-12 references; 515 papers, 19% readable in full via open access, the rest abstract or title only). One model (Claude Opus 5.5) writes, extracts, audits and judges; guards, a claim-level audit with one repair round, and scoring are held fixed while the strategy varies: direct reading (all papers in one prompt), an agentic curator, an evidence graph, a case table, recall-then-verify, a memory-only control, three add-ons and four 'reading better' variants of direct reading. The primary endpoint is coverage of 6,652 atomic facts split once, blind to drafts, from OMIM's variant-centred allelic-variant text deposited in ClinVar, scored only in draft paragraphs citing the fact's paper. Main results: hiding the full text of the same papers lowers direct reading's coverage from 79.8% to 36.1% (46 entries, +43.7 points, better on 45); at the main settings the agent and evidence graph are within about 0.6 points of direct reading and the case table trails by 1.9; in a matched ablation on 38 entries the evidence graph leads by 1.8; a frozen-prompt completeness pass adds 2.6 points on 38 held-out entries; the audit catches citation swaps and single-value substitutions but, because a claim takes the best verdict over its cited papers, not added irrelevant citations, and it cannot see omissions. No person validated any judgement.
Strengths: Clean within-paper manipulation of access (Sec. 4.1, Fig. 2a, App. Table 23): the same 46 entries and papers are rewritten with full text hidden, compared like for like with no arm repaired; full text adds 43.7 points (95% CI 38.3 to 49.1), better on 45 of 46 entries. This is the paper's most convincing result and gives a useful magnitude for anyone building literature-curation pipelines.

Nuisance variables are tightly controlled: one model, identical guards for every strategy (ontology identifiers only from search candidates, HGNC normalisation, removal of recalled cross-references, mandatory citation of a supplied paper), one audit and one scoring procedure (Sec. 3.2, Table 4). Fact lists are split once without sight of any draft and reused for every strategy, and the earlier per-draft splitting is kept as a secondary row that preserves the ordering (Sec. 3.3, Table 6).

Statistical reporting is well above the norm: paired bootstrap intervals, better/worse/tied counts, exact sign tests (the reported values check out, e.g. 31/48 gives p = 0.071 and 31/42 gives p = 0.242), Holm adjustment for secondary measures, a replicate-noise yardstick from three full replicates on 30 entries (App. E, Table 20), an intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis (Table 11), a symmetric completion rule, and an explicit primary/secondary/post hoc/exploratory label for every analysis (Sec. 3.3, Tables 2-3).

The stated/not-stated decomposition (Fig. 2b-c, Fig. 3, Table 19) makes the headroom explicit: reading strategies convey 91.0-94.4% of facts the supplied text states and 5.5-6.9% of facts it does not, no better than the memory-only control (8.2%). This explains why strategies can separate only by a few points in this regime and directly motivates the completeness pass.

The completeness-pass experiment follows good practice: prompts written on three training entries and frozen before 41 held-out entries were run; the gain is localised where it should be (stated full-text facts, +4.5 points) with no change on unstated facts (Fig. 3b, Table 29), and a post hoc sensitivity analysis for stopped revisions is reported rather than hidden (Table 31).

The audit stress test yields a concrete, transferable finding for cited-generation systems: the best-verdict-over-cited-papers rule hides added irrelevant citations (0 of 30 flagged, although the added paper's own verdict was 'unsupported' for 176 of 176 claims; Table 49), and 4-7% of (claim, cited paper) pairs in real multi-citation paragraphs are unsupported (Table 52).

Contamination is addressed with a memory-only control by creation era, including 2026 entries not used in development (Fig. 5, App. M.2): memory-only coverage falls from 24.1% (600000 band) to 5.7-7.0% and its gene F1 to 41.2% and 30.0%, while direct reading stays near 52%.

Reporting is unusually candid: deviations from design, a frameshift-naming bug fixed before the reported results, an earlier analysis that had put the evidence graph 2.1 points below direct reading (App. M.4), every safety-filter stop, cost per strategy and in total (Table 12; about $3,587), and release of per-entry drafts, verdicts and scores.
Weaknesses: No human validation of any judgement on which the primary endpoint rests: fact splitting, present/partly/absent marks, the 'stated' classification and all audit verdicts are made by the writer's own model family (Sec. 3.3; Limitation i). The only reliability evidence is self-consistency (95.7% per-fact agreement between two judgings; Table 20). Because most strategy differences are 0.5-3 points, a small strategy-dependent judge bias (self-preference, or differential crediting of paraphrase versus extracted quotes) could create or erase them. App. M.3, where the same model re-judged the paper as supporting the draft in 22 of 37 draft-reference contradictions, shows that judge-reference disagreements are unresolved. For a paper whose contribution is a benchmark and a measurement, an expert-labelled stratified sample with chance-corrected agreement is necessary.

One writer model in a regime that favours direct reading. All entries have 2-12 references that fit one prompt, 81% of papers are abstract or title only, and a frontier long-context model writes everything (Sec. 3.1, Sec. 5). Extract-first designs are motivated mainly by context limits and many long papers; the tier that would test this (App. K.2, 76-148 references) completed 0 of 4 entries, and the 30-75-reference tier is reported without findings (Sec. 4.4). The 'strategy matters little' conclusion is therefore established only where it is most expected, and no second model family, in particular no smaller-context writer, was run (Limitation ii).

The size of the access effect is largely determined by how the reference is built. The reference is OMIM's variant-centred allelic-variant text, whose content (variants, zygosity, counts, families) lives mostly in full papers; Fig. 2b shows the supplied text states 76% of facts about full-text papers but 26% of those about abstract-only papers. Hiding full text therefore removes most creditable content, and the 43.7-point magnitude is a property of this reference as much as of reading. The paper concedes the direction is expected; its contribution is the magnitude, which does not obviously generalise. The access effect on the independent HPO-synopsis reference is not reported for the hidden-full-text experiment.

The matched-ablation result is presented as a settings effect but is mostly an entry-set effect. The abstract and Introduction highlight that with settings matched the evidence graph leads by 1.8 points (0.4 to 3.3) on 38 entries. App. F states that the ablation reuses the main run's drafts and that on these same 38 entries the main-settings evidence graph already led by +1.0 (-0.8 to +2.9); Table 22 gives the settings change itself as graph matched minus graph = +0.8 (-0.5 to +2.1; 18/12). App. E likewise shows the graph ahead in all three replicates on the 30-entry subset but -0.5 on the 93 main entries. A settings effect is clearly supported only for the case table (+2.1, +1.1 to +3.2; Table 22). The claim that 'the order of close designs depends on settings' should be restated as dependence on the entry set (and, for the case table, on extraction settings), and the main text should report this decomposition.

Missing data from safety-filter stops are non-random, unexplained and repeatedly decisive: 7 of 100 entries are dropped from the main comparison (Table 5), 3 and 6 of 41 from the two completeness arms, 10 of 30 of the 2026 entries, 4 of 4 large entries and every STORM entry (Tables 2-3). Restricting comparisons to entries every arm completed conditions on a strategy-dependent outcome; the reading-better gain turns to -3.5 and -4.8 points under zero imputation (Table 31). Zero imputation is extreme, but the paper cannot say whether stops correlate with entry features that also predict coverage (Limitation ii).

Limited reusability as a benchmark. The fixed fact lists cannot be redistributed (Sec. 3.1 'Reuse'; Ethics statement), the stability of a fresh split by the same procedure was not measured, and a different splitting procedure shifts levels by 2-5 points (Table 6). Third parties therefore cannot score against the reported denominators or compare with the reported numbers, which weakens contribution (1).

Development-set reuse and forking paths. The main strategies were developed on the entries they are evaluated on (Limitation viii). The combined 'checklist with completeness pass' arm was designed after the other three arms' held-out results were seen and is then evaluated, as primary, on the same held-out entries (Sec. 4.3; App. I). Several claim-bearing analyses are post hoc (the stated/not-stated restrictions, the no-repair rescoring of the hidden-full-text experiment, the stopped-entry sensitivity analysis), and the primary endpoint is not adjusted across the five comparisons with direct reading (Sec. 3.3).

Non-inferiority claims without margins or intervals. The abstract's 'without lowering the share of claims judged supported' rests on 20 audited entries (97.2% against 97.0%; Table 32) with no interval or pre-set margin. Sec. 4.2 is appropriately careful that 'not distinguishable' is not an equivalence claim, but the abstract's 'not distinguishable from reading all papers in one prompt' reads more strongly than the evidence supports.

The primary endpoint covers a narrow slice of what a draft says: about 24% of a direct-reading draft's statements have a counterpart in the reference (App. H), narrative sections of phenotype entries are not compared, and the audit checks fidelity, not correctness (Sec. 4.5). Most draft content is therefore evaluated only by the same-model audit, whose sensitivity estimates come from small planted samples (2-8 items per qualifier rule; Fig. 4).

Clarity suffers from extreme density: heavily qualified sentences, many coined terms (like for like, repaired/unrepaired, completes, stated, pooled versus mean over entries), and 53 pages with 54 tables; Sec. 4.4 compresses four experiments into one paragraph with no findings. Small inconsistencies: Sec. 4.5 speaks of six classes of 30 items each with deleted negations all caught, whereas Fig. 4 shows negation as an 8-item sub-rule of the 30-item qualifier class; Table 1's matched block gives variant precision for the case table but '-' for the evidence graph without explanation, while App. F lists precision for other graph variants; Sec. 4.1 hides 91 papers in 49 entries although 96 papers are readable in full, without accounting for the other 5.

Methodological novelty and relevance to the ICLR audience are modest: no new method is proposed (Sec. 2 says so), the measurement lessons of Sec. 5 are mostly established good practice, and the released-pipeline comparison is too small and too altered (PaperQA2 without its agent, GraphRAG on 4 entries, STORM on none; Sec. 4.4, App. J) to inform the strategy question beyond this harness.
Questions: Can you have domain experts label a stratified sample (for example 300-500 facts across strategies, access levels and stated/not-stated classes) and a sample of audit verdicts, and report chance-corrected agreement with the model judge? Do the main strategy differences and the stated/not-stated contrast survive on expert labels?

Can you rerun the main comparison, or at least the 38-entry ablation set, with a second writer family and a judge from another family, including a smaller-context writer for which extract-first designs should matter?

Given App. F and Table 22 (main-settings evidence graph +1.0 on the same 38 entries; matched minus main-settings graph +0.8 with an interval that includes zero), will you revise the abstract, Introduction and Sec. 4.2 to attribute the evidence graph's lead mainly to entry selection rather than to settings?
Why does the hidden-full-text experiment hide 91 papers in 49 entries when 96 of the 515 papers are readable in full? What happened to the other five?

Which entries does the safety filter stop (topic, size, full-text share, creation era)? Do the main conclusions hold under bounds or imputations less extreme than zero, for example imputing the entry's direct-reading score or a per-entry worst/best case?
What is the effect of hiding full text on the HPO-synopsis measures, whose reference is largely curated independently of OMIM's variant text?

How much do levels and paired differences move between two independent fact splits made by the same procedure? Could you release fact identifiers with hashed content, or a scoring service, so that others can score against your denominators without redistributing curator text?

Using the per-paper verdicts you recovered for 80-88% of entries (Table 52), how many real paragraphs would an 'any cited paper fails' rule flag, and how many of those are genuine over-citations on manual inspection?
Can you report an interval or a pre-specified non-inferiority margin for the completeness pass's share of claims judged supported, and audit all 38 compared entries rather than 20?
Limitations: The authors' limitations section (Sec. 5, i-xi) is thorough and candid, including the absence of human validation, a single model family, no large-entry results, the narrow reference and development on evaluation entries.

Not stated plainly enough: the ordering of close strategies depends on which entries are averaged (App. E: graph ahead on the 30-entry subset in all replicates, behind on the 93; App. F: graph +1.0 on the 38 ablation entries at main settings), not only on settings.
The magnitude of the access effect is specific to a variant-centred reference whose facts live mostly in full text; it should be presented as conditional on this reference.

The single model's safety filter determines which entries and systems can be compared (main set, reading-better arms, 2026 entries, large entries, STORM), so every comparison set is shaped by an opaque, model-specific process.
Third parties cannot reproduce scores on the same denominators because the fact lists are not redistributable and split stability is unmeasured.

Generated drafts concern human genetic disease; the disclaimer that they are unvalidated machine drafts, not clinical guidance or OMIM content (Ethics statement), should remain prominent in any released harness.
